## Introduction

This part covers the B-spline basis manipulation tools provided by
the 'BsplineQuantReg' package. B-splines are a powerful tool for
nonparametric regression and function approximation. The package
provides a comprehensive set of functions for building, manipulating,
and evaluating B-spline bases. The calculations are standard and follow
authors such as de Boor or Schumaker.

<!-- slide: 1 — Introduction -->

## Building a B-spline basis

### Basic construction

The primary function for building a B-spline basis is
"Bspline_base()", which takes an extended knot sequence and returns the
basis functions in piecewise polynomial form.
\tiny
see the help: base	
Coefficients in the local bases, in the form of an 3-d array [j,nu,coeff], j : the number of the spline in the basis, nu: the number of the interval in the extended notation, coeff : the coefficients in decreasing (matlab) order convention on the local bases (t-s_nu)^l, l=3.2.1 base[j,,] is a matrix of piecewise polynomial function compatible with the pp-form.
\normalsize
```{r build-basis, echo=TRUE}
# Extended knot sequence for cubic B-splines on [0, 5]
# with internal knots at 1, 2, 3, 4
sn <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)

# Build the basis
basis <- Bspline_base(sn, degree = 3)
```


### Basic construction: Inspect the basis structure
```{r basis_cnst}
str(basis[1:4])
```

<!-- slide: 2 — Basic construction -->

### Visualising the basis

The `view_basis()` function provides a quick visualisation of all basis
functions.

```{r view-basis, fig.cap="Cubic B-spline basis on [0, 5] with internal knots at 1, 2, 3, 4.", fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="80%"}
view_basis(basis)
```

<!-- slide: 3 — Visualising the basis -->

### Understanding the extended knot sequence
\small
For a B-spline of degree $d$ with $k_n$ intervals, the extended knot
sequence has length $k_n + 1 + 2d$:
```{r extended-knots , echo=TRUE}
# d = 3, kn = 5 (intervals: [0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [4, 5])
# Length: 5 + 1 + 6 = 12
sn_example <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
# The first and last d knots are repeated to enforce boundary conditions
basis_example <- Bspline_base(sn_example, degree = 3)
cat("Number of basis functions:", basis_example$n_splines, "\n")
cat("Effective knots:", basis_example$knot, "\n")
```

<!-- slide: 4 — Understanding the extended knot sequence -->

### Visualising different degrees : prepare the bases

```{r prep-degrees, fig.cap="B-spline bases of degrees 0 (top), 1 (middle) and 2 (bottom).", fig.width=8, fig.height=8, out.width="80%"}
# Build bases for degrees 0 to 7
# (endpoints repeated d+1 times)
bases <- lapply(0:7, function(d) {
  sn <- c(rep(0, d + 1), 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, rep(5, d + 1))
  Bspline_base(sn, degree = d)
})
names(bases) <- paste0("deg", 0:7)
```

### Visualising different degrees : the view with view_basis()
```{r view_deg, out.height="80%", echo=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 4), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 1), cex.main=0.8)

for (d in 0:7) {
  view_basis(bases[[d + 1]],x_values = (1:499)/100)
#  title(main = paste("Degree", d))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1), cex.main=1)
```

## Differentiating a B-spline basis
\tiny
The `Bspline_base_deriv()` function computes the basis of derivatives
of a B-spline basis.
```{r basis-deriv}
basis_der1 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 1)
basis_der2 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 2)
basis_der3 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 3)
```
The degree of the differentiated basis is lowered accordingly
```{r}
cat("Original degree:", basis$degree, "\n")
cat("1st derivative degree:", basis_der1$degree, "\n")
cat("2nd derivative degree:", basis_der2$degree, "\n")
cat("3rd derivative degree:", basis_der3$degree, "\n")
```

<!-- slide: 8 — Differentiating a B-spline basis -->

### Visualising derivative bases
\tiny
```{r view-deriv-bases, fig.cap="Original basis and its first three derivative bases.", out.width="80%", out.height="65%"}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
view_basis(basis, main = "Original basis (deg 3)")
view_basis(basis_der1, main = "1st derivative basis (deg 2)")
view_basis(basis_der2, main = "2nd derivative basis (deg 1)")
view_basis(basis_der3, main = "3rd derivative basis (deg 0)")
```

## B-spline objects

### What is a B-spline object?
B-spline objets are the outputs of all the main functions "SplineCubicQuant()", "SplineQuarticQuant()", etc. and
"SplinePolynQuant()".

A B-spline object in 'BsplineQuantReg' is a list with **three components**:

- `knot`: the effective knot partition (endpoints included, **not** the
  extended sequence);
- `degree`: the polynomial degree $d$;
- `coeff`: the vector of coefficients on the B-spline basis.
\small
This representation is **compatible with the Matlab and Python
representations** of B-splines: the same three components are used to
describe a spline in 'BsplineQuantRegpy' and in the Matlab toolbox. 
(but scipy uses the extended knot representation)
\tiny
**Note**: The extreme knots must be repeated **$d + 1$ times** in the extended
sequence used by "Bspline_base()".

<!-- slide: N — What is a B-spline object? -->

## Create a B-spline. Method 1: from a bare list
"make_spline()" accepts a list with
`knot`, `degree` and `coeff`:

```{r bspline-method2, echo=TRUE}
tn <- c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
bs <- make_spline(list(
  knot   = tn,
  degree = 3,
  coeff  = c(1, -2, 3, -1, 2, 1, 0, 0.5)
))
```

### Create a B-spline. Method 2: from a basis
This is an equivalent way to build a B-spline object in "BsplineQuantReg'.

Build the basis with "Bspline_base()",
then attach the coefficients:
The coefficients, knots, degree stay attached to the object.

```{r bspline-method1, echo=TRUE}
sn <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
basis <- Bspline_base(sn, degree = 3)
basis$coeff <- c(1, -2, 3, -1, 2, 1, 0, 0.5)
```





### Methods to create a B-spline — compare
The two objects are equivalent and evaluate to the same function:

```{r bspline-method-equivalence, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="80%", echo=TRUE}
x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 200)
y1 <- spline_eval(bs, x)
y2 <- spline_eval(basis, x)

cat("Max |y1 - y2| =", max(abs(y1 - y2)), "\n")
```


### Methods to create a B-spline — view
\tiny
```{r create_view, out.height="75%"}
plot(x, y1, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "black",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)",
     main = "Two equivalent B-spline constructions")
lines(x, y2, lwd = 2, col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("From a bare list","From Bspline_base()"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

<!-- slide: N+1 — Two ways to create a B-spline -->

### Callable and non-callable B-splines
A B-spline can be stored in two forms:

- **Non-callable** (`non_callable_spline`): a plain list, accessed with
  `$knot`, `$degree`, `$coeff`. Evaluation requires "spline_eval()".
- **Callable** (`callable_spline`): an R function, evaluated directly as
  `f(x)`.
The "make_spline()" function switches between the two:

### Callable and non-callable B-splines: switch
\small
```{r callable-noncallable, echo=TRUE}
bs_nc <- make_spline(bs, callable = FALSE)
class(bs_nc)   

bs_c  <- make_spline(bs_nc, callable = TRUE)
class(bs_c)    

# Same evaluation, two syntaxes
x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)
y_nc <- spline_eval(bs_nc, x)
y_c  <- bs_c(x)

cat("Max |y_nc - y_c| =", max(abs(y_nc - y_c)), "\n")
```


### Getting the parameters of a B-spline object: non callable spline directly
\footnotesize
The "get_parameter()" function allows to obtain the parameters of both non-callable and callable Bsplines,
as well as their equivalent pp-object (callable and non callable)
A non-callable B-spline is simply a list, and its parameters can be obtained directly.
```{r get-param,echo=FALSE}
cat(" obtain the parameters directly from the non callable bspline\n")
bs_nc$knot
bs_nc$coeff
bs_nc$degree
cat("for bs_nc (non callable)")
get_parameters(bs_nc)
```


### Getting the parameters of a B-spline object : callable spline
\footnotesize
```{r}
cat("for bs_c (callable)")
get_parameters(bs_c)
```

### Getting the parameters of a B-spline object : 
```{r}

```


### Alterniveley print the informations
\tiny
```{r info_print}
print(bs_nc)

print(bs_c)
```

### Evaluating a B-spline: description and code
\small
Two functions are available for evaluation:

- "spline_eval(bs, x)": evaluates the spline (linear combination of
  basis functions) at the points `x`.
- "bs_direct(basis, x)": evaluates the **basis matrix** at `x`, of size
  `n_splines` × `length(x)`.

The two are related by matrix multiplication:
\tiny
```{r eval-bspline, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, echo=TRUE}
x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)

# Direct evaluation
y_direct <- spline_eval(bs, x)

# Via the basis matrix
Bmat <- bs_direct(Bspline_base(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5),
                               degree = 3), x)
y_matrix <- t(Bmat) %*% bs_nc$coeff

cat("Max |y_direct - y_matrix| =", max(abs(y_direct - y_matrix)), "\n")
```


### Evaluating a B-spline: the view

\tiny
```{r eval_view1, out.height="80%"}
plot(x, y_direct, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "black",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)",
     main = "spline_eval() vs bs_direct() %*% coeff")
lines(x, y_matrix, lwd = 2, col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("spline_eval()", "bs_direct() %*% coeff"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

<!-- slide: N+3 — Evaluating a B-spline -->

## Converting a Bspline to PP-form
### Use of "Bsplinetopp()" : example code
The piecewise polynomial (PP) form represents the spline **piece by
piece**, as a polynomial on each interval. Conversion is done with
"Bsplinetopp()":

```{r convert-pp}
pp_nc <- Bsplinetopp(bs, callable = FALSE)
class(pp_nc)   

pp_c <- Bsplinetopp(bs, callable = TRUE)
class(pp_c)    
```

The PP-form can be evaluated with "evalpp()" (non-callable) or directly
(callable). The two representations of the spline **coincide**:


### Use of "Bsplinetopp()" : example comparison
```{r pp-coincide,echo=TRUE}
x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 200)
y_bs <- spline_eval(bs, x)
y_pp <- evalpp(pp_nc, x)
y_pc <- pp_c(x)

cat("Max |y_bs - evalpp| =", max(abs(y_bs - y_pp)), "\n")
cat("Max |y_bs - callable| =", max(abs(y_bs - y_pc)), "\n")
```

### Use of "Bsplinetopp()" : example view
```{r bsplinetopp-view, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, echo=FALSE}
plot(x, y_bs, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "black",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)",
     main = "B-spline evaluation vs PP-form evaluation")
lines(x, y_pp, lwd = 2, col = "red", lty = 2)
lines(x, y_pc, lwd = 2, col = "blue", lty = 3)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("spline_eval()", "evalpp()", "PP callable"),
       col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

<!-- slide: N+4 — Converting to PP-form -->

### Use of "Bsplinetopp()" : example comparison again
\tiny
```{r bspline-to-pp, echo=TRUE}
pp <- Bsplinetopp(bs, Bsbasis = basis$basis, callable = FALSE)
print(pp)

x_plot<-x
y_pp <- evalpp(pp, x_plot)
y <- spline_eval(bs, x_plot)
```

\small
```{r}
# Should match the original B-spline

cat( "max(abs(y - y_pp))", max(abs(y - y_pp)) )

```

<!-- slide: 13 — PP-form conversion -->

pp_call <- Bsplinetopp(bs, callable = TRUE)
class(pp_call)  
y_call <- pp_call(x_plot)

## Differentiating a B-spline function
There are at least four methods to compute evaluate derivatives of a B-spline function at given values with this package.
In a given configuration with $k$ knots $t_\nu$ including extremities, and
degree $d \in \mathbb{N}$, the B-spline basis is
$(\pi_j(x))_{j=1,\dots,N}$, with $N = k + d - 1$.

A spline $f(x)$ with this degree and these knots is a vector written on
the basis. The derivative is obtained by differentiating each term of the sum:

$$
f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_j \pi_j(x). \Rightarrow  f'(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_j \pi_j'(x).
$$

### First and second method for derivatives : description
**The first method.** Each B-spline $\pi_\nu$ is described with its
coefficients on the local power basis for each of its pieces. When
computing the basis, these local coefficients are stored in the
`BB$base[, nu, ]` array. The differentiation is done on these local
polynomial pieces. The `der` parameter is passed through the
"spline_eval()" function to compute a derivative of the basis.


**The second method**
The differentiation is a decomposition of the function spline_eval when the parameter der is activated.
Step by step : differentiating the Bspline basis, then evaluate the basis at the given values, and at last reconstruct the derivative $f'(x)$
with these values and the same coefficients $\alpha_i$ as those of $f(x)$ in its writing on the basis.

### Third method: description
**Third method: description**
$\pi_{d,j}$ be the $j$-th spline of degree $d$, and $\pi_{d,j}'$ be the $j$-th spline of degree $d-1$ 
$$
f'(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N-1} \alpha_j \pi_{d,j}'(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_j' \pi_{d-1,j}(x), 
$$
$\alpha_j'$:   the coefficients of f'(x) on the basis of degree $d-1$.
Formula for $\pi_{d,j}'$: that derived by de Boor, implemented in "Bspline_deriv()".
$$\alpha_i'=\frac{\alpha_{j+1}-\alpha_j}{(t_{i+d}-t_i)/d}$$

### The fourth method : description
**The fourth method**
When computing its PP-form, the spline is written as a sum of disjointed piecewise polynomials of degree $d$.

$$
f(x) = \sum_{\nu=1}^{k-1} p_\nu(x) \mathbb{1}_{\left[t_\nu, t_{\nu+1}\right[}, 
$$
It suffices to differentiate each polynomial piece $p_\nu$.  In practice, the Bspline is written as a pp-object with Bsplinetopp(),  and differentiated  with the  pp_deriv() function.

<!-- slide: 9 — Differentiating a B-spline function : introduction -->

### Method 1: "spline_eval()" with the `der` parameter : construction
The simplest method is to use "spline_eval()" with the "der" argument.
This function calculates the derivative of the B-spline basis, then the
values of the differentiated basis, and finally evaluates the function.

```{r eval-deriv, fig.cap="A random cubic B-spline function and its first three derivatives.", fig.width=8, fig.height=8, out.width="80%", echo=TRUE}
bs_function<-bs # bs is  the preceding example 

x_plot <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)
y  <- spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot, der = 0)
y1 <- spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot, der = 1)
y2 <- spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot, der = 2)
y3 <- spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot, der = 3)
```

### Method 1: "spline_eval()" with the `der` parameter : view the plots
```{r eval_plot, echo=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(x_plot, y,  type = "l", main = "Function",      xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")
plot(x_plot, y1, type = "l", main = "1st derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'(x)")
plot(x_plot, y2, type = "l", main = "2nd derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f''(x)")
plot(x_plot, y3, type = "l", main = "3rd derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'''(x)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

<!-- slide: 10 — Method 1: spline_eval() with der -->


### Method 2: Evaluation using basis derivatives : the code construction of a derivative spline
This method follows the same path as "spline_eval()":

1. Compute the derivative basis.
2. Evaluate the basis at points using "bs_direct()".
3. Use matrix multiplication with the coefficients.

```{r step-by-step, fig.cap="Step-by-step derivative evaluation: all methods coincide.", fig.width=8, fig.height=8, out.width="80%", echo=TRUE}
# Step 1: Compute the derivative basis (derivative order = 1)
basis_der1 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 1)
# Step 2: Evaluate the derivative basis at points using bs_direct

x_plot <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)
Bvalues_der1 <- bs_direct(basis_der1, x_plot)
```


### Method 2: Evaluation using basis derivatives : the code
\small
```{r splibe_code, echo=TRUE}
# Step 3: Compute the derivative values using matrix multiplication
y_der1 <- t(Bvalues_der1) %*% basis$coeff

# Step 4: Compare with spline_eval (direct method)
cat("Maximum difference:", max(abs(y_der1 - y1)), "\n")
basis_der2 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 2)
Bvalues_der2 <- bs_direct(basis_der2, x_plot)
y_der2 <- t(Bvalues_der2) %*% basis$coeff
basis_der3 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis, der = 3)
Bvalues_der3 <- bs_direct(basis_der3, x_plot)
y_der3 <- t(Bvalues_der3) %*% basis$coeff
```

```{r}
### Method 2: comparison method 2 - method 1
cat("Maximum difference |y_der2-y2|:", max(abs(y_der2 - y2)), "\n")
cat("Maximum difference |y_der3-y3|:", max(abs(y_der3 - y3)), "\n")
```

### Method 2: Step-by-step evaluation using basis derivatives : view the spline
```{r spline_view, echo=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(x_plot, spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot), type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "Function", xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")
grid()
plot(x_plot, y_der1, type = "l", col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2,
     main = "1st derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'(x)")
grid()
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 3)
plot(x_plot, y_der2, type = "l", col = "purple", lwd = 2,
     main = "2nd derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f''(x)")
grid()
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 3)
plot(x_plot, y_der3, type = "l", col = "orange", lwd = 2,
     main = "3rd derivative", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'''(x)")
grid()
abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

<!-- slide: 12 — Method 3: Step-by-step evaluation -->


### Method 3: "Bspline_deriv()" for derivative coefficients
The second method computes the coefficients of the $d$-th derivative
B-spline directly on a B-spline basis, with the new degree
$d_{\text{new}} = d - \text{der}$.
\small
```{r bspline-deriv}
der1_func <- Bspline_deriv(bs_function, der = 1)
der2_func <- Bspline_deriv(bs_function, der = 2)

y1_coeff <- spline_eval(der1_func, x_plot)
y2_coeff <- spline_eval(der2_func, x_plot)

# Both methods should give the same result
cat("max(abs(y1 - y1_coeff))",max(abs(y1 - y1_coeff)),"  ")
cat("max(abs(y2 - y2_coeff))",max(abs(y2 - y2_coeff)))
```

<!-- slide: 11 — Method 2: Bspline_deriv() -->
### Method 4: Differentiating the PP-form with "pp_deriv()" : the method

The fourth method relies on the PP-form representation of the spline.
Since, on each interval, the spline coincides with a polynomial $p_\nu$,
its derivative is simply the derivative of each $p_\nu$. The function
"pp_deriv()" implements this piecewise differentiation:

1. Convert the B-spline to its PP-form with "Bsplinetopp()".
2. Differentiate each piece with "pp_deriv()".
3. Evaluate the resulting PP-form with "evalpp()" (or directly, if the
   PP object is callable).

### Method 4: Differentiating the PP-form with "pp_deriv()" : the code
```{r pp-deriv-code ,echo=TRUE}
# Convert the B-spline to PP-form (non-callable, for clarity)
pp <- Bsplinetopp(bs_function, callable = FALSE)

# Differentiate each piece
pp_d1 <- pp_deriv(pp, der = 1)
pp_d2 <- pp_deriv(pp, der = 2)
pp_d3 <- pp_deriv(pp, der = 3)

# Evaluate the differentiated PP-forms on the same grid
y_pp<- evalpp(pp, x_plot)
y1_pp <- evalpp(pp_d1, x_plot)
y2_pp <- evalpp(pp_d2, x_plot)
y3_pp <- evalpp(pp_d3, x_plot)
```


<!-- slide: 13 — Method 4: pp_deriv() : the code -->

### Method 4: Differentiating the PP-form with "pp_deriv()" : the view
\tiny
```{r pp-deriv-view2, fig.cap="The four differentiation methods coincide.", fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="80%",echo=FALSE}

# All methods should give the same result
cat("Max |y - y_pp| =", max(abs(spline_eval(bs_function, x_plot) - y_pp)),"   ", "Max |y1 - y1_pp| =", max(abs(y1 - y1_pp)))
cat("Max |y2 - y2_pp| =", max(abs(y2 - y2_pp)),"  ","Max |y3 - y3_pp| =", max(abs(y3 - y3_pp)))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(x_plot, y_der1, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2,
     main = "1st derivative: two methods", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'(x)")
lines(x_plot, y1_pp, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("spline_eval(der = 1)", "pp_deriv(der = 1)"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

plot(x_plot, y_der2, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2,
     main = "2nd derivative: two methods", xlab = "x", ylab = "f''(x)")
lines(x_plot, y2_pp, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("spline_eval(der = 2)", "pp_deriv(der = 2)"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

plot(x_plot, y_der3, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2,
     main = "3rd derivative: two methods", xlab = "x", ylab = "f'''(x)")
lines(x_plot, y3_pp, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("spline_eval(der = 3)", "pp_deriv(der = 3)"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

# Fourth panel: errors on a log scale
plot(x_plot, abs(y_der1 - y1_pp), type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "Numerical differences", xlab = "x", ylab = "|error|",
     ylim = c(1e-16, max(abs(y3 - y3_pp))))
lines(x_plot, abs(y_der2 - y2_pp), col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
lines(x_plot, abs(y_der3 - y3_pp), col = "orange", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd"),
       col = c("blue", "darkgreen", "orange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

<!-- slide: 14 — Method 4: pp_deriv() : the view -->



## Derivatives at knots
Use  `Spline_der_knot()` function to compute derivative values at knot
points rapidly. This is a very simple function, but with limited use.

```{r der-knot}
der_knots <- Spline_der_knot(basis, der = 1)
print(head(der_knots))
```

<!-- slide: 20 — Derivatives at knots -->



## Coherence of derivative evaluation methods with other degree 

### degree 5 for coherence of the derivative methods example code
```{r degree5-coherence, fig.cap="First derivative of a degree-5 B-spline: the three methods coincide.", fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="80%", out.height="65%"}
sn5 <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5)
basis5 <- Bspline_base(sn5, degree = 5)
basis5$coeff <- c(1, -2, 3, -1, 2, 1, 0, -1, 2, 5)

x <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 100)

y1 <- spline_eval(basis5, x, der = 1)

der_basis <- Bspline_deriv(basis5, der = 1)
y2 <- spline_eval(der_basis, x)

der_basis2 <- Bspline_base_deriv(basis5, der = 1)
Bvals <- bs_direct(der_basis2, x)
y3 <- t(Bvals) %*% basis5$coeff
```

### degree 5 for coherence of the derivative methodds : example view
\tiny
```{r diff_compar, echo=FALSE}
cat( "Max differences:  " ,"Method 1 vs Method 2:", max(abs(y1 - y2)), "  Method 1 vs Method 3:", max(abs(y1 - y3)) ) 

cat("Method 2 vs Method 3: " , max(abs(y2 - y3) ) )

plot(x, y1, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2,
     main = "First derivative - all methods coincide (deg 5)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "f'(x)")
lines(x, y2, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(x, y3, col = "green", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("spline_eval(der=1)", "Bspline_deriv", "Step-by-step"),
       col = c("blue", "red", "green"), lty = c(1, 2, 3), lwd = 2)
grid()
```

## Advanced: knot multiplicity and regularity

Knot multiplicity controls the smoothness of B-splines at knot points.
The regularity at a knot is determined by the multiplicity $m$ and the
degree $d$: the spline is $C^{d - m}$ at that knot.

### Creating B-splines with multiple knots

```{r multiplicity, fig.cap="Cubic B-spline basis with a double knot at x = 3.", fig.width=8, fig.height=5, out.width="80%"}
sn_mult <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
basis_mult <- Bspline_base(sn_mult, degree = 3)

view_basis(basis_mult)
abline(v = 3, col = "orange", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

<!-- slide: 18 — Creating B-splines with multiple knots -->

### Effect of multiplicity on regularity : example code

```{r multiplicity-effect, fig.cap="B-spline bases with multiplicities 1, 2, 3 and 4 at x = 3.", fig.width=8, fig.height=10, out.width="80%"}
sn1 <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
sn2 <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
sn3 <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)
sn4 <- c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5)

basis1 <- Bspline_base(sn1, degree = 3)
basis2 <- Bspline_base(sn2, degree = 3)
basis3 <- Bspline_base(sn3, degree = 3)
basis4 <- Bspline_base(sn4, degree = 3)
```

### Effect of multiplicity on regularity : example view
\tiny  
view_basis(basis) with basis= basis1, basis2, bsasis3, basis4

```{r mult_view, echo=FALSE}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
view_basis(basis1, main = "m=1 (C^2 at x=3)")
view_basis(basis2, main = "m=2 (C^1 at x=3)")
view_basis(basis3, main = "m=3 (C^0 at x=3)")
view_basis(basis4, main = "m=4 (discontinuous at x=3)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```



<!-- slide: 21 — Coherence of derivative evaluation methods -->

## Summary

| Feature | Function | Description |
|---------|----------|-------------|
| Build basis | `Bspline_base()` | Create B-spline basis |
| View basis | `view_basis()` | Visualise basis functions |
| Differentiate basis | `Bspline_base_deriv()` | Compute derivative basis |
| Differentiate function | `spline_eval(der = ...)` | Evaluate derivatives |
| Derivative coefficients | `Bspline_deriv()` | Get derivative B-spline |
| PP conversion | `Bsplinetopp()` | Convert to PP form |
| Callable spline | `make_spline()` | Create callable function |
| Extract params | `get_parameters()` | Get parameters from callable |
| Derivatives at knots | `Spline_der_knot()` | Efficient knot derivatives |

All B-spline functions are implemented in pure R and support B-splines
of any degree (greater than 0), with full derivative and PP-form
capabilities. The limitation to degree 4 applies only to regression
with constraints over intervals.
